I am always bothered by people who claim a label simply because they've dabbled in something and in no way take it seriously, such as this charlatan.

A vital component to running is nutrition. Hitting the streets and "running" - and as others have pointed out this woman is taking extreme liberties with that term - is only one part of being a runner. If you want to call yourself a runner you need to embrace all of the aspects of running: nutrition, apparel, proper rest (e.g., sleeping right), training regimens, and putting in the miles. I spend more time as a runner on the other aspects than I do actually on the road. When I limit myself to two beers at happy hour, I'm doing it because I'm a runner and I have a training session in the morning.

Another aspect of successful running is humility. Do you know how much I've improved by myself? The answer is not much. How much have I improved thanks to the guidance (and training companionship) from others? The answer this time is quite different. Other runners have helped me along my way because I stay humble. They don't help me because I encourage magazines to write about how great it is to stay exactly where I am for years at a time by disregarding every part of the running lifestyle except "training" in which I never push myself to prepare myself for races I'll never do.

Last week I attended an education night hosted by my local running store in which we discussed whether or not to carry water on race day. A belt or vest with 22 ounces of water weighs less than 5 pounds but that was a compelling argument against carrying any hydration, preferring to rely on aid stations exclusively. Even a 1% reduction in (human) body weight is a consideration for runners who take their craft seriously.

Slogging along with an extra 100 pounds of dead weight on your body is not what a runner does. Doing so, therefore, immediately tells me that the subject is not serious about the sport and therefore has no right to claim the title "runner," and doing so voluntarily despite it insults me personally.

I don't have a problem with people who start their running lifestyle with pounds to lose. I do have a problem with people who never bother losing them and call themselves a runner anyway.

Not a car salesman but do know one thing. A lot of people will say to look up the value of the car you are thinking of buying on kelley blue book, but most dealers don't use that. Galves is better and is actually used by many dealers to price their cars. Costs 10 bucks for, I think, a day, but you just need it to look up the cars you are interested in. This way, you know the wholesale value of the car before discussing price with them.

Getting a deal does depend on the car you are looking into getting. The dealer has more margin on a bigger truck with a lot of options and is able to give a discount and still make money. But on a compact without any options there just isn't any margin and would be harder to get a lower price.

Don't look at the monthly payment. Many things can be changed to get you a lower payment but not lower the price of the car.
